metadata.title: Lecture 19 : Cayley graphs
metadata.abstract_summary: This lecture discusses Cayley graphs, which are labeled, directed graphs on vertex set G with an edge labeled by s from g to h when h = gs for s ∈S. The lecture also covers commutators and the commutator subgroup, and provides examples and proofs of various properties of these concepts.

sections.heading: Lecture 19 : Cayley graphs
sections.text: Lecturer: Clinton Conley Scribe: Rajeev Godse 1 (Right) Cayley graphs Given a group G and subsets S ⊆ G , the corresponding (right) Cayley graph , Cay( G, S ), is the labeled, directed graph on vertex set G with an edge labeled by s from g to h when h = gs for s ∈ S . Examples : 1. G = Z , S = { 1 } 0 1 2 − 1 − 2 . . . . . . 1 1 1 1 1 1 2. G = Z , S = { 2 , 3 } . Similar to above. 3. G = ⟨ a, b : a 2 = 1 , b 5 = 1 , aba = b − 1 ⟩ , S = { a, b } . You can work it out for yourself, but we get two “circles” acting in opposite directions, connected at each vertex bidirectionally by reflections. 4. G = F 2 = ⟨ a, b ⟩ , S = { a, b } . The Cayley graph is an infinite 4-regular tree, as each reduced word represents a sequence of operations such that the inverse of a previous operation does not occur after that operation. 5. G = ⟨ a, b : aba − 1 b − 1 = e ⟩ , S = { a, b } . The Cayley graph gives us good intuition that G ≃ Z 2 . 2

claims.text: The corresponding (right) Cayley graph, Cay(G, S), is the labeled, directed graph on vertex set G with an edge labeled by s from g to h when h = gs for s ∈ S.
Examples of Cayley graphs include G = Z, S = {1} and G = Z, S = {2, 3}.
The Cayley graph of G = F2 = ⟨a, b⟩, S = {a, b} is an infinite 4-regular tree.
The Cayley graph of G = ⟨a, b : aba−1b−1 = e⟩, S = {a, b} gives good intuition that G ≃ Z2.

sections.heading: Commutators (again!)
sections.text: Recall, for g, h ∈ G , their commutator is [ g, h ] = ghg − 1 h − 1 , and [ g, h ] = 1 ⇐⇒ gh = hg by extreme obviousness. Further recall the commutator subgroup , or derived subgroup , G ′ = [ G, G ], is ⟨ [ a, b ] : a, b ∈ G ⟩ . More generally, for A, B ⊆ G , define [ A, B ] = ⟨ [ a, b ] : a ∈ A, b ∈ B ⟩ .

sections.heading: As a universal property
sections.text: The abelianization of a group G is the quotient map q : G → G/G ′ . It is characterized by the following universal property : Given any abelian group A and any homomorphism ϕ : G → A , there exists a unique homomorphism ψ : G/G ′ → A such that ϕ = ψ ◦ q . Proof : Note that by the first IM theorem, G/ ker( ϕ ) ≃ im( ϕ ) ≤ A , so G/ ker( ϕ ) is abelian. Accordingly, G ′ ≤ ker( ϕ ). Thus, whenever gG ′ = hG ′ , we know that ϕ ( g ) = ϕ ( h ) since g − 1 h ∈ G ′ ≤ ker( ϕ ). We may thus unambiguously define ψ : G/G ′ → A by gG ′ �→ ϕ ( g ). Certainly, it works, so ψ is unique. 2
